title: Threading and concurrency primitives -- lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, thread pool
exp: async/await (Day 2) handles the common case of I/O-bound concurrency. This day covers what happens when you need actual thread-safety for shared mutable state, or CPU-bound parallelism -- a different problem async/await alone doesn't solve.
pts: `lock (obj)` is syntactic sugar over Monitor.Enter/Monitor.Exit -- it ensures only one thread executes the protected block at a time. Always lock on a private, readonly object reference dedicated to that purpose -- never lock on `this`, a public field, or a string literal, since external code could accidentally lock on the same object and cause unexpected contention or deadlocks.

A lock statement CANNOT contain an `await` -- holding a lock across an asynchronous suspension point is a compile error (in modern C#) because the thread that re-enters after the await may not be the same thread that acquired the lock, breaking Monitor's thread-affinity requirement.

SemaphoreSlim is the async-compatible alternative to lock when you need to limit concurrent access and potentially await inside the protected section -- `await semaphore.WaitAsync()` then `semaphore.Release()` in a finally block.

Interlocked.Increment/Decrement/CompareExchange perform atomic operations on a single variable without needing a full lock -- far cheaper than Monitor for simple counter increments shared across threads, since it compiles to a single CPU-level atomic instruction rather than acquiring and releasing a lock.

The Thread Pool is a shared, managed pool of worker threads that both Task.Run() and the async/await machinery's continuations use by default -- understanding this explains why blocking a thread pool thread (calling .Result or .Wait() on a Task) can starve the pool under load, since it ties up a thread that could otherwise serve other work.

Task.Run() is for CPU-bound work you want to offload to a background thread. It is NOT the right tool for I/O-bound work -- wrapping an I/O call in Task.Run() just occupies a thread pool thread waiting on I/O that could have completed without any dedicated thread at all via true async I/O (like HttpClient's native async methods).

Parallel.For / Parallel.ForEach partition a CPU-bound loop across multiple threads automatically -- appropriate for pure computation over a large in-memory collection, not for I/O-bound work where async/await is the correct tool instead.

Race conditions and deadlocks are different failure modes: a race condition produces inconsistent/wrong results because operations interleave unpredictably; a deadlock produces a hang because two or more threads are each waiting on a resource the other holds, with neither able to proceed.
pr: Write a method with a race condition on a shared counter using no synchronization, then fix it two ways: with lock and with Interlocked

qa.q: Why can't a lock statement contain an await, and what should you use instead when you need both?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Monitor (which lock is sugar for) has thread affinity -- the same thread that calls Monitor.Enter must call Monitor.Exit. After an await, execution may resume on a completely different thread pool thread than the one that entered the lock, which would violate this requirement. The compiler prevents this with an error. SemaphoreSlim is the correct alternative -- its WaitAsync()/Release() pair has no thread-affinity requirement, making it safe to use around code that awaits.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: Why is Interlocked.Increment preferred over a full lock for a simple shared counter?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Interlocked operations compile down to a single atomic CPU instruction (like a hardware-level compare-and-swap), avoiding the overhead of acquiring and releasing a Monitor lock entirely -- no kernel-level synchronization object, no possibility of contention causing a thread to be suspended. For simple operations on a single variable (increment, decrement, compare-and-swap), Interlocked is both simpler and measurably faster than wrapping the same operation in a lock block.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: Why is wrapping an I/O-bound call in Task.Run() considered a mistake, even though it 'works'?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Task.Run() schedules the wrapped work onto a thread pool thread. If that work is I/O-bound (an HTTP call, a database query), the thread pool thread sits idle, blocked waiting for the I/O to complete, when it could have been freed to do other work entirely -- true async I/O (via HttpClient's async methods, for example) doesn't consume a thread at all while waiting, since the OS notifies .NET via a completion port when the I/O finishes. Task.Run() around I/O work doesn't add parallelism; it just wastes a thread pool thread that could serve other requests, which becomes a real scalability problem under load in a server application.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: What is the difference between a race condition and a deadlock, and what specific symptom distinguishes them in production?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared mutable state without proper synchronization, producing inconsistent or incorrect results depending on unpredictable timing -- the symptom is wrong data, not a hang, and it's often intermittent and hard to reproduce. A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are each waiting on a resource the other holds, with neither able to proceed -- the symptom is the application (or a specific request) hanging indefinitely with no progress and no exception thrown, until a timeout (if any) eventually fires.
